Salesforce Solution Engineering

Build & deploy custom demos with an AI agent, GitHub, and Heroku

A four-phase workflow to go from zero to a live microsite connected to your Salesforce demo org — no DevOps background required.

Slack Request AI Agent (Claude / Cursor / Codex) GitHub Heroku Private Space Salesforce Org
1
Get Heroku access via Slack
Request to join your team’s Private Space — one-time setup
Join #heroku-for-sales-enablement in Slack
Run the Request to Join Heroku Team workflow in that channel
OU: AMER TMT (or your region)
Justification: “Hosting executive discussion sites built with AI coding agents”
Once approved, sign in to Heroku via the Okta tile (heroku-sso)
access granted ↓
2
Build your demo content with an AI agent
Generate a microsite, AgentForce demo connections, or discussion site
Choose your AI coding agent
ClaudeCursorMeshMeshGitHub Codex
Use a skill or blueprint file to guide the agent — example: HAV Demo Blueprint (SKILL.md) and Solution Blueprint
Store Salesforce org credentials in a .env file (managed via Terminal on Mac or PowerShell on PC — never commit this file)
Tip: Keep .env in your .gitignore so credentials are never pushed to GitHub.
content ready ↓
3
Store and version your content on GitHub
Create a repo, generate a fine-grained access token, push your code
Sign up at github.com if you don’t have an account, then create a new repository (public or private)
Generate a fine-grained personal access token (PAT)
Avatar → Settings → Developer Settings → Personal Access Tokens → Fine-grained tokens
Set an expiration date and select which repos can be accessed
Repository permissions needed: Read (artifact metadata & metadata) + Read & Write (code, pull requests, workflows)
GitHub: Create a new repository
GitHub: Fine-grained personal access tokens list
GitHub: PAT detail — repository permissions
Copy and save your token immediately — GitHub only shows it once. Store it in a secure note or 1Password. You’ll need to regenerate it if lost.
Push changes to a feature branch, then merge into your deploy branch (often main — confirm with your team)
code pushed ↓
4
Deploy to Heroku and go live
Create an app in your Private Space and wire it to GitHub for auto-deploys
In Heroku, switch your active context to se-amer-tmt (or your team) — you will not be able to create apps in the default Personal space
Create a new app — select Private Space (not Common Runtime) and choose se-amer-tmt-internal in Virginia, US
Heroku: Switch to your team's Private Space
Heroku: Create new app — New dropdown
Heroku: Create new app in Private Space
Go to the Deploy tab → select GitHub as deployment method → connect your GitHub account (one-time)
Search for your repo (e.g., siemens-knowledge-enablement) and click Connect
Heroku: Deploy tab — select GitHub as deployment method
Heroku: Search for your repo and connect it
Select your deploy branch and click Enable Automatic Deploys — every merge to that branch triggers a new deployment
Heroku: Connected repo — enable Automatic Deploys
Heroku: Automatic deploys enabled from main
Heroku: More menu — View Logs for troubleshooting
Click Open app (internal) in the top-right of the Heroku dashboard to visit your deployed site
Private Space URL fix: If you see a “bad gateway” error, add -internal after herokuapp in the URL.
Example: your-app.herokuappapp-internal.com → your-app.herokuapp-internal.com
Heroku: Open app (internal) — use the -internal URL for Private Space apps
Troubleshooting deploys: Before a manual deploy, open More → View Logs first. Copy any errors and paste them into your AI agent to diagnose and fix.
Auto-deploys on merge Manual deploy available View Logs for errors
